summary: Tipaza, the capital of Tipaza Province in Algeria, was called Tipasa under Roman rule; the modern town was founded in 1857 and is known for its ancient ruins and sandy littoral. Originally a Punic trading-post, it became a Roman military colony and Christian hub before successive destruction and reconstruction, while its ruins now underpin its importance as a tourist destination.

deviceA.name: Tipaza longwave transmitter
specs: Broadcasts French language Channel 3 programs from the Algerian Broadcasting Company on 252 kHz.
Reception extends to many parts of Europe.
Transmission power: 1500 kW during the day and 750 kW at night.
Antenna: 355-meter tall guyed mast, the second-tallest structure of Algeria.
deviceA.availability: Broadcasts resumed at 252 kHz after an outage beginning March 17, 2014.

coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: Ancient Rome conquered the Punic trading-post; Claudius converted it into a military colony for the conquest of the kingdoms of Mauretania, and it subsequently became the municipium Colonia Aelia Tipasensis.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The modern town founded in 1857 is distinct chronologically from ancient Tipasa, which underwent destruction, reconstruction and later resettlement.
The transmitter's broadcasting history includes an interruption beginning March 17, 2014, followed by resumed service at 252 kHz.

fitAdvice: Tipaza's ancient ruins are the principal basis of its importance as a tourist destination in modern Algeria.
Tipaza and its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, the largest Berber-speaking group of western Algeria; the majority of the Bouriba family also reside in this area.
